text.p: He struck out during the O.J. Simpson criminal trial, but now Mark Fuhrman is striking back.

The disgraced former Los Angeles detective whose lying over whether he used racist words played a major role in Simpson's acquittal in 1995 is trying to set the record straight, reclaim his reputation and make money at the same time.

Whether his mega-blitz of publicity succeeds only time will tell, but so far he seems to be getting attention, showing up on television denying he is a racist and shouting down Simpson lawyer Alan Dershowitz, who accused him of trying to frame the ex-football star by planting a bloody glove on his estate.

He has told his side to eagerly attentive media heavyweights and has been written up in People magazine. His book, "Murder in Brentwood," is climbing the bestseller charts with 350,000 copies in print and the publisher says it will be No. 3 by next week.

Fuhrman quit the Los Angeles Police Department and pleaded no contest to perjury charges for denying at the 1995 trial that he had used racial epithets. A witness produced tapes from when they had worked on a a screenplay together in which he repeatedly used the word "nigger."

But now he is staging a comeback and the secret to his success so far is elementary -- instead of indulging in self-pity and writing a defensive mea culpa as many expected him to do, Fuhrman has gone on the attack. Although he is almost gentle on the "Dream Team" defence lawyers who vilified him, he lashes into the Los Angeles police as a bunch of "Keystone Kops" who botched what he calls the "crime of the century."

He says police missed a bloody fingerprint on the keylatch on the back gate of the South Bundy home where Nicole Brown Simpson and Ron Goldman were murdered on June 13, 1994. He says they also missed a pair of dark sweat pants in a dryer at Simpson's nearby Rockingham estate that could have matched up with fibers found in his car, an empty knife box in his bathroom and a bloodstain on a light switch there.

"I would have taken the whole back gate down to the police lab," Fuhrman said in a recent interview. "I once took a whole door down there on a minor crime. If I can't explain it, if it could be evidence, if it looks odd or strange, it becomes evidence. I can always get rid of it but it might mean something later on, in a week or a month."

Shortly after he and Roberts arrived at the murder scene, the case was handed over to two more senior detectives, Philip Vannater and Tom Lange, and Fuhrman was sent to Simpson's home, where he said he discovered a bloody glove similiar to one left at the scene of the crime.

The defence accused Fuhrman of planting the glove to frame Simpson. But Fuhrman says the discovery of the fingerprint clears him of planting evidence because why would someone want to plant a glove if there was already a print available that could lead to the killer's identity.
Lange and Vannater say no print was found at Bundy.
